title: 3 hours of Story Time
summary: A 3.5-hour story-time stream that opens with a short Q&A (program hopping, mini cuts, partials, Kroc rows, tennis elbow, joint supplements) and then moves into life stories: bad haircuts, a violent week in Paris during the 2019 strikes, his first day and years in America, academia, a haunted dorm, being banned from an all-you-can-eat sushi place, a French government summer job, a cross-country move with his home gym, and several near-death experiences. He also gives an update on his new School of Strategy coaching work.
claims: If neck training gives you headaches, using bands tends to reduce the problem
Someone paralyzed by program hopping should stop consuming YouTube information and stick to one training style; almost every methodology works if done long enough
Mini cuts can never really hurt, but a young lifter should not do too many of them
He likes partials for forearms and does partials for biceps on preacher curls; for other exercises he always uses full range of motion because it feels better
Tuna is an excellent protein source, but watch the mercury content
There is no single right way to do the Kroc row, but keep the weight in front of the body, use pronated wrists rather than semi-supinated, and keep the torso as upright as possible without shrugging
To deal with tennis elbow from chin-ups, warm up properly with triceps isolation exercises first (he also made a tendon guide)
Keep training during exams; even 15 minutes a day helps brain capacity, so don't decide the time is better spent elsewhere
His favourite joint supplement is MSM powder: it tastes terrible but he uses it to keep ligaments and joints strong
To fix a flat-looking physique, build the thickness muscles: chest, arms and traps
He doesn't care about strength and isn't proud of any lift, but is happy with how strong he is on biceps movements
He wants to do a 90-day non-stop rice bucket forearm challenge before making a video on it, but stopped for lack of time; a sand bucket would be too abrasive, causing cuts and dry hands
He once made a pillow stuffed with rice to support his lumbar spine during back problems
During the Paris strike trip he weighed 110 kg and was so heavy that pedaling a kid's bike up any slight incline wrecked him
As an overweight young man he cut his own hair short on the sides and longer on top, trying to create a visual illusion to look less fat
The Paris trip to see a dying relative made him realize life had no inherent meaning and he had to make his own, which led him to start the YouTube channel
Leaving home alone at 20 to study in the US made him a man because he had to make his own decisions and mistakes; he thinks every young man needs to go through this
In grad school he taught 1-9 pm, trained in the gym from 9 to 11 pm, then worked on his master's in the office until 3-4 am
All-you-can-eat sushi places delay plates so you lose appetite; eating fast lets you eat more, which is also why slow eating and chewing is advised for fat loss
He and his crew would lift, fast for 24 hours, then eat an all-you-can-eat sushi buffet out of business; he once finished about 35 yakitori alone and got banned
Charm and getting people on your side matter more than intelligence, work or talent; a sympathetic administrator saved his job and scholarship
Worrying about national politics you can't control destroys people's lives; do your best, see what happens tomorrow and react
His garage home gym was about $10,000 of equipment weighing thousands of pounds, which made moving across the country a major problem
He got a serious concussion playing American football in France, kept playing on autopilot, lost his bearings in the subway after, and quit football to protect his brain
He now coaches about 30 people in his School of Strategy plus 15 in philosophy and literature, working from about 9 am to 1 am, and calls it the best choice of his life
You can tell a partner's quality by how she reacts to your shenanigans; his wife laughed at his accidental bowl cut where an ex dumped him over a drunk mullet
exercises: weight in front of body; pronated wrists; torso as upright as possible without shrugging
